**Surat al-Isra'** (The Night Journey)

It is Meccan, according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: except for eight verses, from His saying ﴿And indeed they came close to tempting you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ to His saying ﴿...a helper with authority﴾.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa﴾. As for His saying ﴿Glory be (subhana)﴾, there are two interpretations concerning it.

The first: it is the declaration of God's transcendence above every evil. It was also said: rather, He declared Himself free of having anyone else exert influence in the night journey of His servant.

The second: its meaning is that God cleared Him of evil. The poet has said:

*I said, when his boasting came to me: "Glory be to (subhana) 'Alqamah the boaster!"*

This is an expression of exaltation that is not fitting for anyone other than God, and the poet used it in an unusual manner. It derives from *al-sabh* (swimming/gliding) in the sense of exaltation, which is moving through it to the furthest extremes.

Aban ibn Tha'labah mentioned that it is a word in the Nabataean language (*shubhanak*). Al-Kalbi and Muqatil mentioned that *subhana* in this context means "wonder," and the meaning of the verse is: "A wonder at the One who took His servant by night." Sibawayh and Qutrub agreed with this interpretation and took the verse of poetry as evidence for it, saying that its meaning is "a wonder at 'Alqamah the boaster."

The reasoning behind this interpretation is that when witnessing a wonder becomes the cause of glorification, glorification becomes an expression of wonder, so it is said "wonder." A similar example is the saying of Bashshar:

*She sends forth glorification (tasbihah) wherever she turns, and she stirs the heart of the beholder with trembling.*

The word *tasbih* occurs in speech in four ways:

The first: it is used to mean prayer. Of this is His saying: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify (al-musabbihin)...﴾ [al-Saffat: 143], meaning, of those who pray.

The second: it is used to mean making an exception. As some have said regarding His saying: ﴿Did I not tell you, "Why do you not glorify (tusabbihun)?"﴾ [al-Qalam: 28], meaning, "Why do you not make exception (tastathnun)?"

The third: it means light, based on the report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "The glories (subuhat) of His face would have burned away..." meaning the light of His face.

The fourth: it means declaring transcendence. It was reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about *tasbih* and he said: "The declaring of God's transcendence above evil."

His saying ﴿took His servant﴾ means: took His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). *Al-Sura* is traveling by night. The poet said:

*A night of dew I traveled, and Layth did not reach me with its journey.*

His saying ﴿from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ has two interpretations:

[p-225]

The first: it means from the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), the whole Haram being a masjid.

When he was taken on the night journey, he was sleeping in the house of Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib. Abu Salih reported this from Umm Hani'.

The second: he was taken from the masjid itself, and it was there that he was when he was taken on the night journey. Anas ibn Malik reported this.

Then they differed about the manner of his night journey, on two views.

The first: he was taken with his body and spirit. This was reported by Ibn al-Musayyib, Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, Abu Hurayrah and Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

Those who held this view differed over whether he entered Bayt al-Maqdis and prayed in it or not. Abu Hurayrah reported that he prayed in it with the prophets, then he was ascended (*'uruja bihi*) to the heaven, then he was returned to al-Masjid al-Haram and prayed there the dawn prayer on the morning of that same night.

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman reported that he did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis, did not pray in it, and did not dismount from the Buraq until he was ascended, then he returned to his place.

The second view: the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken with his spirit and not with his body. This was reported from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, who said: "The body of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not lost, but God took him by night with his spirit."

It was reported from Mu'awiyah that he said: "It was a true dream from God, Exalted is He." Al-Hasan used to interpret His saying ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾ [al-Isra': 60] as referring to the ascension (*mi'raj*), because the polytheists denied it and began asking him about Bayt al-Maqdis and what he had seen on the way, so he described it to them. Then he mentioned to them that on the way he saw a covered vessel full of water; he drank the water and then covered it as it was. Then he described to them a caravan of camels that they had on the road to Syria, carrying goods, and that they would arrive on such-and-such a day at sunrise, led by a grey-spotted camel. So they went out on that day to meet it. One of them said: "By God, this is the sun, it has risen but it has not come." Another said: "By God, this is the caravan, led by a grey-spotted camel, just as Muhammad said."

In this there is evidence for the correctness of the first view, that he was taken with his body and spirit.

His saying Exalted is He ﴿to al-Masjid al-Aqsa﴾ means Bayt al-Maqdis, which is the masjid of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both. It was called *al-Aqsa* (the farthest) because of the distance between it and al-Masjid al-Haram.

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾. There are two interpretations concerning it. The first: this means with fruits and flowing rivers.

The second: it means with those prophets and righteous people who were placed around it; for this reason He made it sacred.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God, Exalted is He, says: 'O Syria, you are the chosen land of My lands, and I will drive to you My chosen servants.'"

﴿That We may show him of Our signs﴾. There are two interpretations concerning it. The first: the signs that He showed him on this journey were that He took him by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa in one night, a journey that would take a month.

The second: He showed him, on this journey, signs.

Concerning these signs there are two views. The first: the wonders he was shown, which contain lessons. The second: those of the prophets whom he was shown, until he described them one by one.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: He described Himself, in this situation, as All-Hearing and All-Seeing, although these are among His attributes that are inherent to His essence in all states. This is because He protected His Messenger during his night journey in the darkness of the night, so it does not harm him that he could not see in it; and He heard his supplication and answered him in what he asked. For these two reasons God described Himself as All-Hearing and All-Seeing.

The second: his people all denied him regarding his night journey. So He said: "All-Hearing," meaning of what they say, whether of affirmation or denial; "All-Seeing," meaning of what he did, namely the night journey and the ascension.

The second: that the Book was a guidance for the Children of Israel.

﴿Do not take other than Me as a trustee (wakil)﴾. On this there are three opinions. One: a partner, said by Mujahid.

The second: meaning a lord upon whom they rely in their affairs, said by al-Kalbi.

The third: a guardian (kafil) for their affairs, related by al-Farra'.

﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾, meaning Noah. On this there are two opinions. One: he was called grateful because he would praise Allah, may He be exalted, for his food, said by Salman.

The second: he would not put on a new garment without praising Allah, may He be exalted, when he dressed, said by Qatadah.

It may have two meanings. One: Noah was a grateful servant, so Allah, may He be exalted, made Moses one of his offspring.

The second: Moses was a grateful servant when Allah, may He be exalted, made him one of the offspring of Noah.

**Translation:**

﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book﴾: the meaning of "We decreed" here is "We informed."

It may also bear a second meaning: that it means "We judged." This is the view of Qatadah.

The meaning of His words ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel﴾ is: We decreed against them.

﴿You will surely cause corruption on earth twice﴾. The corruption they committed was their killing of people unjustly, their domination over their wealth by force, and their ruining of their dwellings through transgression.

Regarding those prophets whom they killed in the first corruption, there are two opinions:

(p-229) One: he was Zechariah. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: he was Shi'ya (Isaiah). This is the view of Ibn Ishaq, and that Zechariah died a natural death.

As for the prophet killed in the second corruption, he was Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John the son of Zechariah), according to the consensus. Muqatil said: "Even though between the two there were two hundred and ten years."

﴿So when the promise of the first of them came﴾: that is, the first of the two times of their corruption.

﴿We sent against you servants of Ours, possessors of great might﴾. In His words "We sent" there are two meanings. One: "We left you to them, abandoning you because of your wrongdoing." This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: "We commanded that you be fought, as retribution against you."

Regarding those who were sent against them in this first time, there are five opinions. The first: Jalut (Goliath), whose king was Talut (Saul), until Dawud (David) peace be upon him killed him. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: he was Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar). This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The third: he was Sinharib (Sennacherib). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: they were the Amalekites, who were disbelievers. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: they were a people from the people of Persia who spied on their news. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿So they went through the houses﴾. In this there are five interpretations. The first: it means they walked about and moved between the homes and dwellings. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and it is more emphatic in subjugation.

The second: its meaning is that they trampled through the houses. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"To you I traversed the night with the mounts."*

The third: its meaning is that they killed them among the homes and dwellings. From this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

*"And among us is the one who met with the sword of Muhammad, and so he swept through the enemies, across the ranks of the armies."*

(p-230) The fourth: its meaning is that they searched and sought through the houses. This was said by Abu Ubaydah.

The fifth: its meaning is that they camped among the houses. This was said by Qutrub, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"So we went through their dwellings by force, and we returned with their chieftains bound in chains."*

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then We gave back to you the return [of victory] over them﴾: that is, victory over them. Regarding the manner of this there are three opinions. The first: the Children of Israel raided the king of Babylon and rescued what was in his hands of captives and wealth.

The second: the king of Babylon released whoever was in his hands of captives, and returned what was in his hands of wealth.

The third: it was by the killing of Jalut when Dawud killed him.

﴿And We aided you with wealth and sons﴾ by renewing the blessing upon them.

The second: more in number. The abundance of number makes their enemy fear them. Tubba' ibn Bakr said:

*"So honor Qahtan for a father, and Himyar, honor a people with manpower."*

Qatadah said: "So they remained in it two hundred and ten years, and prophets were sent among them."

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾, because the reward of good returns to them, so that becomes a benefit to them.

﴿And if you do evil, it is against them﴾: that is, the evil returns to them, for what punishment is directed at them. So He encouraged good and warned against evil.

The second: if you return to obedience, We will return to acceptance. This was said by some of the righteous.

The second: a confinement in which they are imprisoned. This was said by Qatadah, derived from ḥaṣr, which is confinement.

The Arabs call a king ḥaṣīr because he is confined by the chamberlains. Labid said:

*"And a gathering of stiff-necked men, as if they were jinn at the door of the ḥaṣīr, standing."*

**Translation:**

﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book﴾: the meaning of "We decreed" here is "We informed."

It may also bear a second meaning: that it means "We judged." This is the view of Qatadah.

The meaning of His words ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel﴾ is: We decreed against them.

﴿You will surely cause corruption on earth twice﴾. The corruption they committed was their killing of people unjustly, their domination over their wealth by force, and their ruining of their dwellings through transgression.

Regarding those prophets whom they killed in the first corruption, there are two opinions:

(p-229) One: he was Zechariah. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: he was Shi'ya (Isaiah). This is the view of Ibn Ishaq, and that Zechariah died a natural death.

As for the prophet killed in the second corruption, he was Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John the son of Zechariah), according to the consensus. Muqatil said: "Even though between the two there were two hundred and ten years."

The second: "We commanded that you be fought, as retribution against you."

Regarding those who were sent against them in this first time, there are five opinions. The first: Jalut (Goliath), whose king was Talut (Saul), until Dawud (David) peace be upon him killed him. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: he was Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar). This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The third: he was Sinharib (Sennacherib). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: they were the Amalekites, who were disbelievers. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: they were a people from the people of Persia who spied on their news. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿So they went through the houses﴾. In this there are five interpretations. The first: it means they walked about and moved between the homes and dwellings. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and it is more emphatic in subjugation.

The second: its meaning is that they trampled through the houses. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"To you I traversed the night with the mounts."*

The third: its meaning is that they killed them among the homes and dwellings. From this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

*"And among us is the one who met with the sword of Muhammad, and so he swept through the enemies, across the ranks of the armies."*

The fifth: its meaning is that they camped among the houses. This was said by Qutrub, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"So we went through their dwellings by force, and we returned with their chieftains bound in chains."*

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then We gave back to you the return [of victory] over them﴾: that is, victory over them. Regarding the manner of this there are three opinions. The first: the Children of Israel raided the king of Babylon and rescued what was in his hands of captives and wealth.

The second: the king of Babylon released whoever was in his hands of captives, and returned what was in his hands of wealth.

The third: it was by the killing of Jalut when Dawud killed him.

﴿And We aided you with wealth and sons﴾ by renewing the blessing upon them.

The second: more in number. The abundance of number makes their enemy fear them. Tubba' ibn Bakr said:

*"So honor Qahtan for a father, and Himyar, honor a people with manpower."*

Qatadah said: "So they remained in it two hundred and ten years, and prophets were sent among them."

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations:

First: the testimony that there is no god but Allah. This is said by al-Kalbi and al-Farra'.

Second: what it contains of commands and prohibitions, which are more correct. This is said by Muqatil.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾. On this there are two interpretations (ta'wil):

The first: that he seeks benefit in the immediate (present) by means of a harm that returns to him in the deferred (future).

The second: that one of them calls down destruction upon himself, or upon his child, and if Allah answered his supplication against this evil just as He answered it for good, he would perish.

﴿And man has always been hasty﴾. On this there are two interpretations:

The first: that he is hasty in supplication against himself, his child, and what pertains to him. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Mujahid.

The second: that it refers to Adam, when the soul was breathed into him and it reached his navel, so he wanted to stand up hastily. This is the statement of Ibrahim and al-Dahhak.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 12:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs; then We effaced the sign of the night﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it is the darkness of the night, in which we cannot see the roads, just as we cannot see what has been erased from the Book. This is among the finest eloquence, and it is the meaning of the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is the black spot that is in the moon. This is the saying of ʿAli and Qatadah, so that the light of the moon is less than the light of the sun, and the night is thereby distinguished from the day.

﴿And We made the sign of the day to be seeing﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it is the sun, shining brightly for sight.

The second: it is "awakening" (mūqiẓah), i.e., making people alert.(p-233)

The Lord, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And every human being We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾. On this there are two opinions.

The first: We have fastened to him his deeds, whether good or evil, in the manner that the Arabs used to say of the (sawanih) al-tayr and (bawarih) al-tayr. The sanih (al-sanih) is the bird that passes from the right side, and it is a good omen; the barih (al-barih) is the bird that passes from the left side, and it is a bad omen. It is attributed to the neck.

The second: his bird is his fortune and his portion, from the saying of the Arabs, "The arrow of so-and-so flew," when his arrow came out and his portion came from it. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open﴾. That is, the record of his bird that is on his neck, of good or evil.

The spreading out of the record that he finds may have two meanings. The first: a hastening of good news for the good deed and a rebuke for the evil deed.

The second: the manifesting of his deed, whether good or evil.

﴿Read your record﴾ may have two meanings. The first: because of the increase in rebuke and reproach that is in reading it.

The second: so that his acknowledgment of it by reading it is against himself.

﴿Sufficient is your soul against you this Day as a reckoner﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: it means a witness.

The second: it means a judge over your deeds, whether good or evil.

Indeed, he has been just to you who made you a reckoner over yourself by your deeds.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 15:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for [the benefit of] his own soul﴾, meaning: for what he obtains of the reward of his obedience.

﴿And whoever goes astray, only goes astray to its detriment﴾, meaning: for what he incurs of the punishment of his disobedience.

﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾. In this there are three aspects. The first: no one will be held to account for the sin of another.

The second: it is not permissible for anyone to be disobeyed on account of the disobedience of another.

The third: no one will be sinful for the sin of another.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: that no one bears the sin of another, and the sinfulness of the doer falls away from him.

﴿And We are not ones who punish until We send a messenger﴾. In this there are two aspects. The first: We would not punish [people] for the religious laws (al-shara'i' al-diniyya) until We send a messenger, and this is the saying of those who claim that reason (al-'aql) precedes revelation (al-shar').

The second: We would not punish [people] for any of the acts of disobedience until We send a messenger calling [to the truth], and this is the saying of those who claim that reason and revelation came together.

Regarding the punishment there are two aspects. The first: the punishment of the Hereafter.

This is the apparent meaning of the saying of Qatada.

The second: punishment by annihilation in this world, and this is the saying of Muqatil.(p-235)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 16:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones﴾ – the verse.

Regarding His saying ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾ there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is "when We decree the destruction of a town."

The second: its meaning is "and when We destroy a town," and His saying ﴿intend﴾ is an extra connective particle (ṣila zā'ida), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a wall that wants to collapse﴾ [al-Kahf: 77]. The third: He intended by the destruction of the town the perishing of its good people and the survival of its wicked ones.

As for ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾, the reading upon which the seven imams of the reciters agree is that amarna is short and light (maqsūr mukhaffaf), and in it there are two aspects. The first: "We command its affluent ones to obey," because God, exalted is He, commands only obedience; ﴿but they transgressed therein﴾, that is, they disobeyed by opposition. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: its meaning is "We sent its arrogant ones (mustakbirīhā)," said by Harun. In the reading of Ubayy it is: "We sent the greatest of its criminals" (akābir mujrimīhā).

In a second reading, ﴿amarna mutrafīhā﴾ with the mīm shaddad (doubled), and its meaning is "We made them rulers, empowered commanders," said by Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi.

In a third reading: āmarna mutrafīhā, with a long vowel, and its meaning is "We increased their number," from the saying of people, "the folk became many" (āmara al-qawmu), since when they are numerous they need a leader who commands them and forbids them. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The best wealth is a mare that is fruitful (muhra ma'mūra) or a field of palms that is pollinated (sikka ma'būra)," meaning abundant in offspring. Labid said:

"If they envy, they will decline; and if they multiply one day, they will come to destruction and misery."

This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatada.

As for ﴿mutrafīhā﴾, there are three interpretations. The first: its tyrants (jabbāruhā), said by al-Hasan.

The second: its leaders (ru'asāʾuhā), said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

The third: its sinners (fussāquhā), said by Mujahid.

The Exalted said: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾. The scholars differed concerning the length of a generation (qarn), and there are three opinions:

First: that it is one hundred and twenty years. This was said by ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Awfa.

Second: that it is one hundred years. This was said by ʿAbd Allah ibn Busr al-Mazini.

(p-237) Third: that it is forty years. Muhammad ibn Sirin related this from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 22–24:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾. Its meaning is "and your Lord has commanded," as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb used to recite (wa-wassa rabbuka, "and your Lord has enjoined"), as related by al-Dahhak. In the codex it was written: "wa-wassa rabbuka," but the scribe joined the waw (and) to the word, so it became ﴿wa-qada rabbuka﴾.

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾. Its meaning is "and He has enjoined kindness to parents," that is, that one should be kind to them through righteousness towards them in deed and in speech.

﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: they reach your old age and the full maturity of your intellect.

The second: they reach their own old age, with weakness and decrepitude.

﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾. That is, when you see from them harm, and they clean away their filth and remove their dirt from you, do not feel impatient, just as they used to clean it away from you when you were young, without impatience.

Regarding the interpretation of ﴿Uff﴾ there are three views. The first: it is every word that is coarse and ugly, as said by Muqatil.

The second: it is the disgust at a thing and a change in its smell, as said by al-Kalbi.

The third: it is a word that indicates weariness and impatience, coming in the manner of imitated sounds.

The Arabs say "uff" and "tuff." Al-uff is the dirt under the fingernails, and al-tuff is what you lift from the ground with your hand of some worthless thing.

﴿And speak to them a noble word﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: gentle.

The second: good.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: this verse and the verse after it were revealed concerning Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 22–24:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾. Its meaning is "and your Lord has commanded," as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb used to recite (wa-wassa rabbuka, "and your Lord has enjoined"), as related by al-Dahhak. In the codex it was written: "wa-wassa rabbuka," but the scribe joined the waw (and) to the word, so it became ﴿wa-qada rabbuka﴾.

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾. Its meaning is "and He has enjoined kindness to parents," that is, that one should be kind to them through righteousness towards them in deed and in speech.

﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: they reach your old age and the full maturity of your intellect.

The second: they reach their own old age, with weakness and decrepitude.

﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾. That is, when you see from them harm, and they clean away their filth and remove their dirt from you, do not feel impatient, just as they used to clean it away from you when you were young, without impatience.

Regarding the interpretation of ﴿Uff﴾ there are three views. The first: it is every word that is coarse and ugly, as said by Muqatil.

The second: it is the disgust at a thing and a change in its smell, as said by al-Kalbi.

The third: it is a word that indicates weariness and impatience, coming in the manner of imitated sounds.

The Arabs say "uff" and "tuff." Al-uff is the dirt under the fingernails, and al-tuff is what you lift from the ground with your hand of some worthless thing.

﴿And speak to them a noble word﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: gentle.

The second: good.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: this verse and the verse after it were revealed concerning Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 25:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who return (to Him in repentance)﴾. Concerning "those who return" (al-awwabin) there are five opinions.

The first: they are the doers of good (al-muhsinun). This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: they are those who pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'. This is the view of Ibn al-Munkadir, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ) (yarfa'uhu).

The third: they are those who pray the Duha (forenoon) prayer. This is the view of 'Awn al-'Uqayli.

The fourth: they are the one who returns from his sin and repents. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

The fifth: they are the one who repents again and again, and whenever he sins, he hastens to repentance. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 26–28:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations.

The first: its meaning is, if you turn away from those among those previously mentioned who ask you, because you are unable to provide for them, ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾, that is, awaiting provision from Him, ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾, that is, promise them good and respond to them with a kind reply. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: its meaning is, if you turn away from those who ask you, out of concern that they would spend it in disobedience, and you withhold it from them, seeking mercy for them, then ﴿speak to them a gentle word﴾, that is, a soft and easy word. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 31–32:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾, meaning burying daughters alive out of fear of poverty.

﴿We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin (khit'an kabiran)﴾. Al-khit' (deliberate sin) is deviating from the correct course intentionally, whereas al-khata' (error) is deviating from it through inadvertence. This is the distinction between khit' and khata'. The poet said:

؎ Al-khit' is an abomination, and righteousness is a supererogation, like a date-pit planted in the ground that is uprooted (tu'tabar).

The second view: khit' is that which is sinful, and khata' is that in which there is no sin. Al-Hasan recited (khita'an) with the long vowel (madd).

The second view: khit' is that which is sinful, and khata' is that in which there is no sin. Al-Hasan recited (khita'an) with the long vowel (madd).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾, meaning, except for that which makes killing due.

﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first: it is retaliation (qawd), as said by Qatadah.

The second: it is the choice between retaliation (qawd), blood money (diyah), or pardon. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak.

The third: ﴿We have certainly given his heir authority﴾ means He has given him support, that he will be aided and given justice concerning his right.

﴿But let him not commit excess in killing﴾. On this there are two opinions. One: the first killer should not commit excess in killing, transgressing and wronging, since the heir of the one killed is supported. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the heir of the one killed should not commit excess in killing.

(p. 241) Regarding his excess there are four opinions. The first: that he kills someone other than the killer. This is the view of Talq ibn Habib.

The second: that he mutilates when exacting retaliation. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: that he kills after accepting blood money. This was said by Yahya.

The fourth: that he kills a group for one person. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Dawud.

﴿Indeed, he has been supported﴾. On this there are two opinions. One: the heir has been supported by being enabled to exact retaliation. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: the one killed has been supported by the killing of his killer. This was said by Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 34–35:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾. He singled out the orphan for mention because he is more in need of that, and greed for his property is greater.

Regarding His words ﴿except in the way that is best﴾ there are two opinions. The first: preserving its principal and developing its yield (thamir, "increase, cultivation") is the meaning, and this is a possibility.

The second: "the way that is best" is trading with his wealth on his behalf.

﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾. Regarding al-ashudd there are two views. The first: it is strength (al-quwwah).

The second: it is the limit (al-muntaha).

As to its time here, there are two opinions. The first: eighteen years.

The second: wet dreams (al-ihtilam) together with soundness of mind and the perception of maturity of judgment (rushd).

﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations:

(p-242) The first: that it refers to the contracts that are concluded between contracting parties, which obligate them to fulfill them. This is the view of Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

The second: that it is the covenant regarding the bequest of the orphan's property, which must be fulfilled.

The third: that it is everything that Allah the Exalted has commanded or forbidden, for it is part of the covenant that must be fulfilled.

﴿Indeed, the covenant was ever being questioned﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects. The first: that the covenant was something demanded (matlub), said by al-Suddi.

The second: that the covenant was itself questioned about, by the one to whom it was made, so the breaker of the covenant is the one questioned.

The third: that the covenant itself is what is questioned, "for what sin was it violated," just as the buried infant girl is asked "for what sin was she killed."

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words: ﴿And weigh with an even balance﴾. Concerning it there are three sayings. The first: that it is the steelyard (al-qabban), said by al-Hasan.

The second: that it is the scale (al-mizan), whether small or large, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is justice (al-adl).

Those who hold this view differ on two opinions. The first: that it is Roman (rumi), said by Mujahid.

The second: that it is Arabic, derived from al-qist (justice), said by Ibn Durustawayh.

﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects. The first: it is better inwardly, so "the good" is what appears, and "the excellence of the interpretation" is what is hidden.

The second: it is better in its consequence, for the ta'wil (interpretation/outcome) of a thing is its consequence.

(p-243) His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations.

The first: its meaning is, do not say what you have no knowledge of. So do not say "I saw" when you did not see, nor "I heard" when you did not hear, nor "I knew" when you did not know. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is, do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are the sons of al-Nadr, of Kinanah; we do not qafw (pursue/accuse) our mother, nor do we disown our father."

The third: that it derives from qiyafah (tracking/tracing), which is following a trace, as if one follows the heel (qafa) of the one who went before. The poet said:

"And like the statues, of lofty noble bearing, within them modesty dwells; they do not stir up qafawa (mutual slander)."

That is, mutual accusation.

﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned about﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: that the human being is the one questioned about the hearing, the sight and the heart, because he uses them to perform obedience and disobedience.

The second: that the hearing, the sight and the heart are questioned about the human being, so that they may be witnesses against him and for him, concerning what he did of obedience and what he committed of disobedience. It is permissible to say "ulā'ika" (those) for non-rational things, as Jarir said:

(p-244)

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days."

The first: al-maraḥ (exultance, arrogant exuberance) is intense joy in falsehood.

The second: that it is vanity in walking (al-khuyala'), said by Qatadah.

The third: that it is insolence and reckless pride (al-baṭar wa al-ashar).

The fourth: that it is a person exceeding his own measure.

The fifth: arrogance in walking (al-takabbur fi al-mashy).

﴿Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], and you will never reach the mountains in height﴾. In it there are two aspects. Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 39–41:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an﴾ has two interpretations. The first: We repeated in this Qur'an the admonitions and parables.

The second: We varied the admonitions, through the difference of their kinds.

﴿That they may remember﴾ has two interpretations. The first: that they may recall the proofs.

(p-245) The second: that they may be guided to the truth.

﴿But it increases them in nothing except aversion﴾ has two interpretations. The first: aversion from the truth and from following it.

The second: aversion from reflection and consideration.

In the speech there is an implied, omitted element, and its estimated form is: "And We have certainly diversified the parables in this Qur'an."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 42–43:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿Say: If there were other gods with Him, as they say, they would surely have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.ﴩ There are two opinions regarding it:

First: They would have sought a path to Him through which they could draw near to Him, because they are partners. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: That they would seek nearness to Him, because they are beneath Him. This was said by Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 42–43:

First: They would have sought a path to Him through which they could draw near to Him, because they are partners. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: That they would seek nearness to Him, because they are beneath Him. This was said by Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿There is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions.

The first: "There is not a thing" among living beings "but it glorifies Him with His praise." As for what is not alive, it does not. This is the view of al-Hasan (al-Basri).

The second: all created things glorify Him, living and non-living, even the creaking of a door. This is the view of Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i).

The third: their glorification is what appears in them of His subtle craftsmanship and wondrous power, which creation cannot match. This compels whoever sees it to glorify and sanctify God, as the poet said:

*She casts forth glorification wherever she turns,*
*and it settles in the breast of the beholder with trembling.*
*As though she were created from the shell of a pearl,*
*every side of her is a face watching.*

[p. 246]

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 45–46:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. There are two interpretations regarding it. The first: that is, We made the Qur'an a barrier so that it would conceal you from them when you recite it.

The second: We made the Qur'an a barrier that keeps them from hearing it when you recite it aloud.

On this basis, there are three opinions. The first: because of their turning away from your recitation, it is as if there were a barrier between you and them preventing them from seeing you. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: the hidden barrier is that God sealed their hearts so that they do not comprehend it. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: it was revealed concerning a people who used to harm him at night when he recited, so God placed between him and them a barrier from the harm. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿Hidden﴾ has two interpretations. The first: the barrier is hidden from you, so you do not see it.

The second: the barrier conceals from you what is behind it, and "hidden" (mastur) here carries the sense of "concealing" (satir). It is also said that it was revealed concerning the Banu 'Abd al-Dar.

﴿Or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾. Regarding this there are four sayings. The first: by it He means the heavens, the earth and the mountains, because of their greatness in souls, as said by Mujahid.

The second: He meant death, for there is nothing greater in the soul of the son of Adam than it, and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

؎ They called upon their God that He might hasten their creation, and for souls, death is a dreadful creation.

The third: He meant the resurrection, for it was the greatest thing in their breasts, as said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: whatever is greatest in your breasts of all that you have considered great of the creation of Allah, the Exalted, for Allah causes you to die, then brings you back to life, then resurrects you, as said by Qatadah.

﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: that is, they will move their heads in mockery and denial. The poet said:

؎ I said to her, "Pray," and she said, "Begone!" and she shook her head at me with a nod.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day He calls you, and you will respond with His praise﴾. Regarding His saying, "He calls you," there are two sayings. The first: it is a call of speech that all people hear, by which Allah calls them to come forth to the place of gathering (al-mahshar).

The second: you will respond in accordance with what the praise of Allah requires of your deeds.

The third: its meaning is that you will rise from your graves by the praise of Allah, not by your own praise.

The fourth: you will respond by His command, as said by Sufyan and Ibn Jurayj.

The third: because of how swiftly they see the return, they think the time spent in the graves was short.

The fourth: between the two blasts the punishment is lifted from them, so they are not punished, and between them is forty years, which they see as brief for their rest; as said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ in denying him.

The second: it is compliance with the commands and prohibitions of Allah, the Exalted. This was said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 54–55:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations.

The first: "If He wills, He will have mercy upon you" through guidance, "or He will punish you" through misguidance.

The second: "If He wills, He will have mercy upon you" by delivering you from your enemies, "or He will punish you" by letting them dominate you. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The third: "If He wills, He will have mercy upon you" through repentance, "or He will punish you" through persistence (in sin). This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And We did not send you over them as a wakil (disposer of affairs)﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations.

The first: We did not appoint you to prevent them from disbelief in Allah, the Exalted, and to compel them to believe in Him.

The second: We did not make you a guarantor (kafil) for them, for which you would be held accountable. This was said by al-Kalbi. The poet said:

Ḍ "I remembered Abu Arwa, so I spent the night as if I were a wakil over restoring the bygone affairs."

Wakil: that is, kafil (guarantor).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 56–57:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord, [to see] which of them would be nearest﴾, the verse. In it there are three opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning a group of jinn whom a people among mankind used to worship. The jinn then embraced Islam, seeking the means of access (al-wasilah) to their Lord, while mankind remained in their disbelief. This was said by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.

The second: they are the angels, whom some tribes of the Arabs used to worship. This is also related from Ibn Mas'ud.

The third: they are Jesus and his mother. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

These are the ones referred to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Call upon those whom you claim besides Him﴾. Its explanation is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: they call upon God, exalted is He, for themselves. The second: they call the servants of God to His obedience.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they seek the means of access to their Lord﴾, and al-wasilah is nearness (al-qurbah). Its interpretation is built upon the two possibilities regarding the calling.

If it is said that it is the calling for themselves, its meaning is that they seek a means to God, exalted is He, through supplication for what they ask.

And if it is said that it is the calling of the servants of God to His obedience, its meaning is that they seek a means for those whom they called to His forgiveness.

﴿Which of them would be nearest﴾: its interpretation according to the first meaning is: which of them is nearest in answering.

Its interpretation according to the second meaning is: which of them is nearest to obedience.

﴿And they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: this hope and fear are in this world. The second: they are in the Hereafter.

If it is said that it is in this world, it admits of two meanings. The first: the hope for mercy is success (tawfiq) and guidance, and the fear of punishment is the severity of trial.

And if it is said that it is in the Hereafter, it admits of two meanings. The first: the hope for mercy is the continuance of blessings, and the fear is of the punishment of the Fire.

The second: the hope for mercy is pardon, and the fear of punishment is the strictness of reckoning.

This hope and fear admit of two meanings. The first: that they are for themselves, if it is said that the original calling was for them. The second: for obedience to God, exalted is He, if it is said that the calling was for others.

It is not impossible that it is general in its scope, both regarding themselves and regarding those whom they called.

Sahl ibn Abdullah said: Hope and fear are two scales upon a person; when they are balanced his states are upright, and if one of them outweighs, the other is nullified.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the hope of the believer and his fear were weighed, they would be balanced."

The second: they are the signs of retribution, a means of frightening (people) away from sins.

The third: they are the changing of conditions, from childhood to youth, then to maturity, then to old age, so that you may take warning from the changing of your own conditions and fear the outcome of your affair. This is the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may God have mercy on him.

(p-253) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when We said to you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people."﴾ On this there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is that His power has encompassed the people, so they are within His grip. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih.

The second: His knowledge has encompassed the people. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The third: that He protected you from the people, so that they would not kill you until you convey the message of your Lord. This was said by al-Hasan, Urwah and Qatadah.

﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first: that it was a vision of the eye on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey) with him from Makkah to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Najih and Ibn Zayd. The trial was the apostasy of a people who had embraced Islam when the Prophet ﷺ informed them that he had been taken on the Night Journey.

The second: that it was a dream in which he saw that he would enter Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ hastened, before the appointed time, on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, and then he turned back. Some people said: "He had said that he would enter it." So his turning back was their trial. This is also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it was a sleeping dream in which he saw people climbing over his pulpit, leaping like monkeys, and this troubled him. This is the saying of Sahl ibn Sa'd.

It is also said that he was never seen laughing fully until he died ﷺ, and then Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

﴿And the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first: that it is the tree of al-Zaqqum, the food of the sinner. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus and Ibn Zayd.

Their trial regarding it was the saying of Abu Jahl and his followers: "Fire consumes trees, so how can it make them grow?!"

(p-254) The second: it is the kushut (dodder) which twines around trees. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: that they are the Jews who banded together against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ along with the confederates. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: "That the Prophet ﷺ saw in his dream people climbing the pulpits, and it grieved him, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed ﴿And the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾." This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The tree is a metaphor for the woman, and the group are the woman's children, like branches of a tree.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on surah 17, verses 61–62:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely I will seize (la-ahtanikanna) his offspring, all but a few﴾. In it there are six interpretations.

The first: its meaning is "I will surely gain dominion over them by overpowering them." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: its meaning is "I will surely lead them astray through seduction."

The third: "I will surely uproot them through seduction."

The fourth: "I will surely win them over (li-astamilanna)." This was said by al-Akhfash.

The fifth: "I will surely lead them to sins just as a beast is led by its jaw (hanak) when a rope is tied to it and pulls it along." The word is an ifti'al form derived from al-hanak (the jaw), referring to the jaw of the beast.

The sixth: its meaning is "I will surely cut them off toward sins." The poet said:

I complain to you of a year that has oppressed us, bringing hardship upon hardship and weakening us.

And it has seized (ihtanakat) our wealth and stripped it bare.

(p-255)

The commentary of God Most High: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them with your voice﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: "and make light of," the view of al-Kalbi and al-Farra'. The second: "and make ignorant." The third: "and humiliate whomever you can," said by Mujahid.

﴿with your voice﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: it is the voice of singing and amusement, said by Mujahid. The second: it is the voice of the mizmar (flute), said by al-Dahhak. The third: it is by your calling them to disobedience of God Most High and to your obedience, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿And urge against them with your cavalry and your infantry﴾. Al-jalb (urging) is driving, with the driver's shouting. In the proverb: "If you cannot overcome, then urge."

His saying ﴿with your cavalry and your infantry﴾ means: with every rider and every walker in the disobedience of God Most High.

﴿And share with them in wealth and children﴾. As for their sharing in wealth, there are four aspects. The first: they are the wealth they acquired from other than its lawful source, said by Mujahid. The second: they are the wealth they spent in disobedience of God Most High, said by al-Hasan. The third: it is what they used to prohibit of the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released), the sa'iba (a beast set free), the wasila (a she-camel or sheep given to idols), and the ham (a stallion camel released after a number of covers), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is what they used to slaughter for their gods, said by al-Dahhak.

As for their sharing in children, there are four aspects. The first: they are children of fornication, said by Mujahid. The second: it is the killing of the buried daughters (al-maw'uda) from among their children, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The third: it is the dyeing of their children in disbelief, until they made them Jews and Christians, said by Qatada. (p-256) The fourth: it is their naming their children slaves of their gods, such as 'Abd Shams, 'Abd al-'Uzza, and 'Abd al-Lat, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 66:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Your Lord is the One who drives the ships for you through the sea﴾. Its meaning is that He makes them run and sends them along. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. The poet said:

Ya ayyuha al-rakibu al-muzjī maṭiyyatahu
sail banī Asadin mā hādhihi al-ṣawtu

("O rider who drives his mount onward, ask the Banu Asad: what is this sound?")

"His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those whom you invoke vanish, except Him﴾. In this there are two meanings.

One: those whom you invoke besides Him are lost (batala), as the Exalted said: ﴿He will not let their deeds go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1], meaning He will nullify them.

The second: its meaning is that those whom you invoke disappear (ghaba), as the Exalted said: ﴿When we are lost (ḍalalna) in the earth﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], meaning, when we are hidden from view."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 68–69:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: He means part of the land, namely the place where they dwell, and He called it its "side" because after the swallowing it becomes a side (of what remains).

The second: they were on the shore of the sea, and the shore of the sea is the side of the land. They felt secure there from the terrors of the sea, so He warned them of what they felt secure from on the land, just as He warned them of what they feared from the sea.

﴿Or He send against you a violent wind (hasib)﴾ has two meanings. The first: it means stones from the sky; this is the view of Qatadah.

The second: al-hasib is a violent wind, so named because it pelts (tuhassibu), that is, throws up pebbles (al-hasba').

And al-qasif is the wind that breaks trees, the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have honoured the children of Adam﴾. Regarding this there are seven interpretations:

First: that is, We honoured them by Our bounties upon them.

Second: We honoured them by making for them intellects and discernment ('uqul wa tamyiz).

Third: by making from among them the best nation brought forth for mankind (khayr ummah ukhrijat li-l-nas).

Fourth: by their eating what they take of food and drink with their hands, while others take it with their mouths. This was said by al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

Fifth: We honoured them by commanding and forbidding (al-amr wa al-nahy).

Sixth: We honoured them by speech and writing (al-kalam wa al-khatt).

Seventh: We honoured them by subjecting all of creation to them.

(p-258) ﴿And We have provided them with good things﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations: First: what Allah has made lawful for them.

Second: what they find good to eat and drink.

Third: that it is the earnings of the worker when it benefits, as said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah.

﴿And We have preferred them above many of those We have created, with a clear preference﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations: First: by dominance and mastery (al-ghalaba wa al-istila').

Second: by reward and recompense (al-thawab wa al-jaza').

Third: by preservation and discernment (al-hifz wa al-tamyiz).

Fourth: by correctness of insight (isabat al-firasa).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 71–72:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿On the Day when We shall call every people by their leader﴾. In this there are five interpretations.

The first: by their prophet. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: by their Book that was sent down to them, containing the commands and prohibitions of God. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The third: by their religion. This is likely the view of Qatadah.

The fourth: by the record of their deeds that they did in the world, good and bad. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: by the one whom they used to follow in the world, so they follow him in good or evil, in truth or falsehood. This is the meaning of the statement of Abu Ubayda.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾ may have four meanings.

The first: whoever is blind in this world to obedience, ﴿he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ to reward.

(p-259) The second: whoever is blind in this world to reflection, ﴿he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ to excuse-making (i'tidhar).

The third: whoever is blind in this world to the truth, ﴿he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ to Paradise.

The fourth: whoever is blind in managing his worldly affairs, he is blind in managing his affairs of the Hereafter, ﴿and further astray from the way﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 73–75:

(p-260) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you, to fabricate other than it against Us﴾. On this there are two views.

The first: what Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to touch the Black Stone (al-Hajar) during his circumambulation (tawaf), and Quraysh prevented him, saying, "We will not let you touch it until you touch our gods." So he spoke to himself and said: "What harm is there if I touch them after they let me touch the Stone, while Allah knows that I dislike them?" Then Allah refused this and revealed this verse to him. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: what Ibn Abbas narrated, that the Thaqif said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give us a year's respite until we take what we offer to our gods. When we have taken it, we will break our gods and become Muslims." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to obey them, and Allah revealed this verse.

﴿to fabricate other than it against Us﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: to claim against Us other than Our revelation. The second: to transgress in Our commands.

﴿And then they would have taken you as a khalil﴾. On this there are two meanings. The first: a friend (sadiq), derived from khullah, with a dammah, which means friendship, because of his collusion with them. The second: a poor man (faqir), derived from khallah, with a fathah, which means poverty, because of his need for them.

His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death﴾. On this there are two views. The first: We would have made you taste double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second: We would have made you taste double the punishment of this world and double the punishment of the Hereafter. This was related by al-Tabari.

Regarding the meaning of "double" (al-di'f) here, there are two views. The first: a share (nasib), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For each there is double﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], meaning a share.

The second: two equivalents, because your sin is greater.

There is also a third view: that "double" is the punishment itself, and it is called "double" because its pain is multiplied. This was said by Aban ibn Taghlib, who recited the verse of the poet:

"Indeed, the killing of Malik, when he separated from me, has me spending the night in a painful double [torment]."

Qatadah said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 78–79:**

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾. As for "the decline of the sun" (duluk al-shams), there are two interpretations. The first is that it refers to its setting, and that the prayer commanded is the Maghrib prayer. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Lamps that are not guided by the ones that lead them, nor by the stars that set and rotate.*

This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Zayd. Mujahid narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the position of Abu Hanifah.

The second is that it refers to its zenith (zawal), and that the prayer commanded is the Zuhr prayer. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of al-Sha'bi from him, and it is the statement of Abu Burdah, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid. It is also the position of al-Shafi'i and Malik, based on the narration of Abu Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm from Ibn Mas'ud and 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Jibril came to me at the decline of the sun when it passed its zenith, and he led me in the Zuhr prayer." The poet said:

*This is the station of the two feet of Rabah, which were stained until the sun (Barah) was rubbed.*

Barah is the name of the sun, and the "ba'" in it is part of the root of the word. Some of the grammarians held that the "ba'" in it is the preposition "ba'" of genitive attachment, and that the name of the sun is Rah.

Whoever makes "duluk" a term for its setting does so because a person rubs his eyes with his palm to see it clearly. Whoever makes it a term for its zenith does so because a person rubs his eyes with his palm due to the intensity of its rays.

It has been said that the original meaning of "duluk" in the language is inclination, and the sun inclines at its zenith and at its setting, so the term applies to each of them.

As for ﴿the darkness of the night﴾ (ghasaq al-layl), there are two interpretations. The first is that it is the appearance of its darkness. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn 'Isa, and from it is the verse of Zuhayr:

*She kept giving with her hands while she was heedless, until the darkening and the ghasaq had come.*

The second is that it is the approach and advance of the night. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The poet said:

*Indeed this night has grown dark... ... ...*

Regarding the prayer that is commanded, there are two views. The first is that it is the Maghrib prayer. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second is that it is the late evening prayer (al-'Isha' al-Akhirah). This was said by Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

Then He said: ﴿And the Qur'an of dawn; indeed, the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. Regarding "Qur'an" (qur'an) there are two interpretations. The first: "Establish the recitation in the dawn prayer." This is the statement of Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

The second: its meaning is the dawn prayer, and it was called "Qur'an" to emphasize the recitation within the prayer. This is the statement of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj.

Regarding ﴿indeed, the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾, there are two views. The first: among its wisdom is that you witness it by attending it in the mosques. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: what is meant by it is what Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it." (p-264) In this there is evidence that it is neither part of the night prayer nor part of the day prayer.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory (nafilah) act for you﴾. As for tahajjud (al-tahajjud), the root hujud is among the words with opposite meanings (asma' al-adhdad); it applies to sleep and to wakefulness. The evidence for its application to wakefulness is the verse of the poet:

*Has she not visited while the people of Mina were sleeping? Would that her phantom returned to Mina.*

The evidence for its application to sleep is the verse of the poet:

*She came to us by night while the companions were sleeping, and she stayed giving with generous gifts.*

As for tahajjud, it is wakefulness. There are two meanings to it. The first: wakefulness through alertness that negates sleep, whether it occurs before sleep or after it. The second: wakefulness after sleep. This was said by al-Aswad ibn 'Alqamah.

In the statement there is an implied, elided element (mudmar mahdhuf), and its estimation is: "So perform tahajjud with the Qur'an and the night vigil as a nafilah," meaning an extra act and addition beyond the obligatory.

Regarding the specification of the Prophet ﷺ in that it is a nafilah for him, there are three aspects. The first: a specification for him, to encourage him towards it and to be foremost in attaining its merit, due to its being specific to his honour. This was said by 'Ali ibn 'Isa.

The second: because it is a merit for him, and an expiation for others. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: because it is obligatory for him, and recommended for others. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station (maqaman mahmudan)﴾. Regarding this there are three statements:

(p-265) The first: that the praiseworthy station is the intercession for people on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

The second: that it is his being seated upon His Throne on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Mujahid.

(p-266) The third: that it is his being given the banner of praise (liwa' al-hamd) on the Day of Resurrection.

It may also admit a fourth statement: that the praiseworthy station is his testimony over his community concerning what they answered him with, whether affirmation or denial, as the Most High said: ﴿And We bring you as a witness over these people﴾ [al-Nisa': 41].

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 80–81:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter a sincere entrance and cause me to exit a sincere exit."﴾ Regarding this there are seven opinions. The first: the "sincere entrance" is his entry into Medina when he emigrated to it, and the "sincere exit" is his departure from Mecca when he emigrated from it. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: "Cause me to enter a sincere entrance" means into Paradise, and "cause me to exit a sincere exit" means from Mecca to Medina. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: "Cause me to enter a sincere entrance" into what You have sent me with of prophethood, and "cause me to exit from it" by conveying the message with a sincere exit. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The fourth: "Cause me to enter Islam with a sincere entrance, and cause me to exit from this world with a sincere exit." This was said by Abu Salih.

The fifth: "Cause me to enter Mecca with a sincere entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sincere exit, safe." This was said by al-Dahhak.

[p. 267] The sixth: "Cause me to enter my grave with a sincere entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sincere exit." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The seventh: "Cause me to enter into what You have commanded me of Your obedience with a sincere entrance, and cause me to exit from what You have forbidden me of Your disobedience with a sincere exit." This was said by some of the later scholars.

Here, "sincerity" (al-sidq) is an expression for righteousness and a good outcome.

﴿And appoint for me from Yourself an authority, a helper.﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: it means a mighty kingdom by which I may subdue the disobedient. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: a clear proof. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: that the authority over the disbelievers is by the sword, and over the hypocrites is by establishing the prescribed punishments (hudud). This was said by al-Hasan.

It may also admit a fourth: that He gather for him the hearts through gentleness and the subduing of bodies through the sword.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And say: "The truth has come, and falsehood has vanished."﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: the truth is the Qur'an, and falsehood is Satan. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: the truth is the worship of God, the Exalted, and falsehood is the worship of idols. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

The third: the truth is jihad, and falsehood is polytheism. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾ That is, going away and perishing. The poet said:

"And indeed his advance has healed my soul and cured its sickness, his conquering attack, by which it did not perish."

Qatadah related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered the Ka'bah and saw the images in it, he ordered a cloth to be soaked with water, and began striking those images with it, erasing them and saying: ﴿The truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾

As the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 193].

Second: It is an angel among the angels who has seventy thousand faces, and for each face there are seventy thousand tongues, glorifying Allah the Exalted with all of that. This was said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

Third: It is the Qur'an. This was said by al-Hasan, as the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a rūḥ (spirit) of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Its meaning would then be that the Qur'an is of the command of Allah the Exalted and His revelation, which was sent down to me, and it is not from me.

Fourth: It is ʿIsa ibn Maryam, who is of the command of Allah the Exalted, and not as the Christians claim, that he is the son of Allah, nor as the Jews fabricate, that he was born out of wedlock.

Fifth: It is the spirit of life, and it is derived from the wind (rīḥ).

Qatadah said: A group of Jews asked him about it, and it was said in their book that if he answers about the rūḥ, he is not a prophet. So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: The rūḥ is of the command of my Lord﴾, and He did not answer them about it. That carries six possible aspects. First: a confirmation of something, if it was in their book.

Second: that they intended by it to cause difficulty, just as they intended to propose signs.

Third: because it may be reached by knowledge through reason without revelation.

Fourth: lest that become a pretext for asking about what does not concern them.

Fifth: as some of the theologians said, that if He had answered them about it and described it as a fine body with which life subsists, it would have come out of the form of prophetic speech and entered the form of the speech of the philosophers.

Sixth: that the purpose of their question about the rūḥ was for it to become clear to them whether it is created (ḥādith) or eternal (qadīm). ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects. One: except a little of the things known to Allah. Two: except a little in accordance with what need calls for, moment by moment.

Regarding those intended by the Exalted's saying ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ there are two opinions. One: that they are the Jews specifically, said by Qatadah. Two: the Prophet ﷺ and all of creation.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 90–93:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring."﴾ Al-tafjir (causing to burst forth) is splitting the earth so that water springs out of it. From it the word al-fajr (dawn) is derived, because it splits open at the column of morning; and from it the word al-fujur (wickedness) is derived, because it is a splitting of the truth by going out into corruption.

Al-yanbu' is the spring from which water wells up. Qatadah and Mujahid said: they asked for springs in their land.

﴿Or you have a garden of palms and grapes﴾: they asked for this in a land where there was no such thing.

﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾: i.e., fragments.

It is recited with the sin sukun and with the sin fathah. Whoever recites it with sukun intends the whole sky; whoever opens the sin takes the meaning to be part of the sky. There are two interpretations of this:

First: it means a space (hayyiz), related by Ibn al-Anbari; perhaps they meant by it the seeing of what is above the sky.

Second: it means pieces (qita'), said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The Arabs say: "Give me a kisfah (piece) of this cloth," meaning a portion of it.

From this comes al-kusuf (eclipse), for the light is cut off from it. According to the second interpretation, it is because it is covered by something that prevents it from being seen.

﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a qabil﴾. In this there are four interpretations:

First: it means each tribe separately; said by al-Hasan.

Second: it means face to face, that we might witness them and see them; said by Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj.

Third: qabil means a guarantor (kafil), and al-qabil is the guarantor, from their saying "taqabbaltu kadha," meaning "I took responsibility for it"; said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Fourth: gathered together, derived from the qaba'il al-ra's (the sutures of the skull) because some of it joins to others; from this the tribes of the Arabs are named, for they gather together; said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Or you have a house of zukhruf﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

First: zukhruf means ornamentation (nuqush); this is the saying of al-Hasan.

Second: it means gold; this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Mujahid said: "I did not know what zukhruf was until we heard in the recitation of 'Abdullah: a house of gold (dhahab)."

Its root is from al-zakhrafah, which is beautifying the appearance, and from it is His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿until when the earth takes on its adornment (zukhrufuha) and is decked out﴾ [Yunus: 24].

Those who asked the Messenger of God ﷺ this were a group of Quraysh. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, Abu Sufyan, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Asad, Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, 'Abdullah ibn Umayyah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and Nubayh and Munabbih, the two sons of al-Hajjaj.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 96–97:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one who is guided﴾. Its meaning: whomever Allah, exalted is He, judges to be guided, he is the one who is guided, through his sincerity and obedience.

﴿And whomever He leaves astray, you will not find for them any protectors apart from Him﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: whomever He judges to be astray, you will not find for him any protectors apart from Him to guide him.

The second: whomever Allah, exalted is He, decrees to be punished, there will not be found for him any helper who prevents him from His punishment.

﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: that this is an expression for hurrying them to Hell, from the Arabs' saying: "The people came upon their faces" when they hastened.

The second: that they will be dragged on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces to Hell, like what is done in this world to one whose humiliation and torment is intended to be extreme.

﴿Blind, dumb, and deaf﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: they will be gathered into the Fire blind in sight, dumb in tongue, and deaf in hearing, so that this will be an increase in their punishment. Then they will see, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and think that they are going to fall into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53], and they will speak, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There they will cry out for destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 13], and they will hear, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will hear its raging and roaring﴾ [al-Furqan: 12]. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: rather, when He says to them, ﴿Be driven away into it, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108], they become blind, not seeing; deaf, not hearing; dumb, not understanding.

The second: their senses remain as they were, and the meaning is: blind to what would gladden them, dumb from speaking what would benefit them, deaf to what would give them pleasure. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾, meaning their place of settling is Hell.

﴿Whenever it subsides, We increase them in blaze﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: whenever it is extinguished, it is kindled again. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: whenever the intensity of its flame subsides, We increase them in blaze and intensity. This was said by al-Dahhak. The poet said:

*And we were like a fire that struck a thicket, it dies down for a while and then blazes up for a while.*

The subsiding of its flame occurs without any decrease in their pain, nor any lightening of their punishment.
