**Commentary on Qur'an 17:105–106**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended﴾ can bear two meanings. The first: that its being sent down is true. The second: that what it contains of commands, prohibitions, promise and threat is true.

﴿And with the truth it descended﴾ can bear two meanings. The first: it descended with Our revelation. The second: it descended upon Our Messenger.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ means: a bringer of good news of Paradise for whoever obeys God, may He be exalted, and a warner of the Fire for whoever disobeys God, may He be exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided﴾ has three meanings. The first: We made distinction in it between truth and falsehood; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: "faraqnahu" with the doubled letter (tashdid, فَرَّقْناهُ), which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. That is, it descended in parts, verse by verse. It is also so in the codex (mushaf) of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "faraqnahu 'alayka" (We divided it upon you).

The third: We detailed it into surahs and distinct verses. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying: ﴿So that you may recite it to the people at a pace﴾ has three interpretations. The first: that is, with deliberation and measured recitation; this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: that some of it would descend, then they would remain (without new revelation) for what God willed, then something else would descend.

The third: that he would pause in reciting it to them, dividing it, one part after another; this was said by Abu Muslim.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts. The first: it was said by al-Kalbi.

That the mention of al-Rahman was rare in the Qur'an, while it was frequent in the Torah. When some Jews embraced Islam, among them Ibn Salam and his companions, the scarcity of the mention of al-Rahman in the Qur'an grieved them, and they loved that it should be mentioned often, so this was revealed.

(p-281) The second: what Ibn Abbas said, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was prostrating and supplicating: 'O Rahman, O Raheem.' The polytheists said: 'This man claims that he has one God, yet he calls upon two.' So this verse was revealed."

﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor recite it in a whisper, but seek a way between that.﴾ Concerning this there are two views. The first: that by "prayer" is meant supplication, and the meaning is: do not raise your supplication aloud nor lower it to a whisper. This is the saying of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and Makhul.

Ibrahim said: "People will surely cease fixing their gaze toward the sky during prayer, or their gaze will not return to them."

The second: that by it is meant the prescribed prayer. Those who held this view differed concerning what was forbidden in loud recitation and in quiet recitation within it, into five sayings. The first: He forbade loud recitation in it, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Makkah used to recite very loudly, so when the polytheists heard him they would revile him. Allah the Exalted forbade him from excessive loudness, and from reciting so quietly that his companions could not hear him, and bade him to seek a way between that. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: He forbade loud recitation throughout all of it, and quiet recitation throughout all of it, and commanded that one recite aloud in the night prayer and quietly in the day prayer.

The third: He was forbidden to recite the tashahhud aloud in the prayer. This was said by Ibn Sirin.

The fourth: He was forbidden to perform the prayer loudly, because he used to pray loudly in Makkah, and the Quraysh would harm him, so he prayed quietly and secretly. Allah commanded him not to pray loudly as he had, nor to pray in a whisper as he had become, and to seek a way between that. This was said by Ikrimah.

The fifth: it means, do not pray loudly, making it beautiful for show in public, nor pray in a whisper, making it bad in secret. Al-Hasan said: "One makes its public form beautiful and its inner state bad."

It was also said: do not pray for show, nor leave it out out of shame.

The first view is more apparent.

It is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, when he prayed, would lower his voice, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Why do you do this?" He said: "I speak privately with my Lord, and He knows my need." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You have done well."

(p-282) And Umar ibn al-Khattab would raise his voice, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Why do you do this?" He said: "I wake the sleeper and drive away the devil." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You have done well." When this verse was revealed, he said to Abu Bakr: "Raise your voice a little," and to Umar: "Lower your voice a little."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And say: Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: He commanded him to praise, to declare Allah exalted above having a son.

The second: to refute what the polytheists associated with Him of offspring.

﴿and who has no partner in the dominion﴾, because He is one, having no partner in dominion or worship.

﴿and who has no protector out of weakness﴾. Concerning this there are three meanings. The first: He has not made an alliance with anyone.

The second: He does not seek anyone's help.

The third: He has no protector from among the Jews and Christians, because they are the most abased of people. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿and magnify Him with all magnificence﴾. Concerning this there are three meanings. The first: describe Him as greater than everything.

The second: magnify Him with exaltation above everything that is not permissible in His attributes.

The third: glorify Him with glorification. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 17, verses 110–111:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts. The first: it was said by al-Kalbi.

That the mention of al-Rahman was rare in the Qur'an, while it was frequent in the Torah. When some Jews embraced Islam, among them Ibn Salam and his companions, the scarcity of the mention of al-Rahman in the Qur'an grieved them, and they loved that it should be mentioned often, so this was revealed.

(p-281) The second: what Ibn Abbas said, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was prostrating and supplicating: 'O Rahman, O Raheem.' The polytheists said: 'This man claims that he has one God, yet he calls upon two.' So this verse was revealed."
